summary.text: Linear regression is a model that estimates the relationship between a response and one or more explanatory variables related through a linear combination.
A model with exactly one explanatory variable is a simple linear regression, while a model with two or more is a multiple linear regression.
Once fitted, the model can be used to predict the response when new values of the explanatory variables arrive without a response.

items.prompt: One model predicts house price from floor area alone. Another predicts it from area, age and distance to town. Which counts as multiple linear regression?

options.label: Both, since price is the response in each
The first, since price is a single response
The second, since it has two or more explanatory variables
Neither, since that needs more than one response

items.explain: A model with exactly one explanatory variable is simple linear regression; two or more makes it multiple linear regression.

items.prompt: A fitted model relates sales to advertising spend. Next month's budget is known but sales are not yet. How can the model help?

options.label: Use the budget in the fitted model to predict the response
Wait for sales to arrive, then refit before any use
Nothing, since the model needs an observed response
Predict the budget from the sales instead

items.explain: If values of the explanatory variables are collected without a response, the fitted model can be used to predict the response.

items.prompt: A dataset contains many very large outliers and the model is fitted by minimizing squared errors. What is the risk?

options.label: The outliers are ignored, because squaring shrinks them
The fit may chase the outliers, as large errors weigh heavily
The fit becomes perfect for all other points
Nothing, since every cost function treats errors alike

items.explain: Squared-error cost gives higher importance to large errors, so the model can fit outliers more than the true data. Cost functions robust to outliers should then be used.

items.prompt: Is every model fitted by least squares a linear model?

options.label: Yes, the two terms mean the same thing
Yes, but only when there is a single predictor
No, least squares only works for straight lines
No, least squares can fit non-linear models too

items.explain: The terms are closely linked but not synonymous: the least squares approach can be used to fit models that are not linear.

items.prompt: A model predicts salary from years of experience and years of education. What does the coefficient on experience describe?

options.label: The total change in salary over a whole career
The correlation between experience and education
The change in salary when both variables move together
The expected salary change per extra year of experience, education held fixed

items.explain: The coefficient is the expected change in the response for a one-unit change in that predictor while the other covariates are held fixed.

items.prompt: In children's data, shoe size alone is strongly linked to reading score, but with age also in the model shoe size adds almost nothing. What does this suggest?

options.label: Another covariate, age, captures the information shoe size carried
The regression has failed and should be discarded
Shoe size causes reading scores to rise
The reading score cannot be a scalar response

items.explain: A unique effect can be nearly zero even when the marginal effect is large, which may mean another covariate captures all the information in that predictor.

beats.prompt: A fitted model links sales to advertising spend. A new advertising budget arrives, but there are no sales figures for it yet. What can be done?
beats.explain: After a model is fitted, additional values of the explanatory variables collected without a response can be used to predict the response.

choices.label: Use the fitted model to predict the sales response

beats.prompt: Sort each description into the model it fits.

left.label: A single scalar predictor x and a single scalar response y
Several or vector-valued predictors, written with a capital X

beats.explain: The number of explanatory variables separates the two: one for simple regression, more for multiple regression.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it is about.

right.label: Fitting by minimizing lack of fit in another norm
The model may fit the outliers more than the true data
A common way to fit a linear regression

beats.explain: Linear regression models are often fitted by least squares, but other fitting criteria exist, and nonlinear regression generalizes the idea.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: A model predicts y from two predictors, x1 and x2.
The fitted coefficient of x1 is 3.
So y is expected to rise by 3 for each one-unit rise in x1 with x2 held fixed.
So x1 on its own, ignoring x2, must also raise y by exactly 3.

beats.explain: A coefficient gives the unique effect with other predictors held fixed. The marginal effect of x1 on its own can be quite different, even nearly zero while the unique effect is large.

beats.idea: Linear regression fits a straight-line relationship to known data, so the response can be predicted from new values and each coefficient read as a change per unit.

paragraphs.heading: Relating a response to predictors
paragraphs.text: Regression describes how one quantity relates to others. The quantity you care about is called the response, or dependent variable. The quantities used to explain it are called explanatory variables, or predictors. In linear regression, the predictors are tied to the response through a linear combination of them.

paragraphs.heading: One predictor or many
paragraphs.text: When there is a single predictor x and a single response y, the model is called simple linear regression. With two or more predictors, it is called multiple linear regression. The model's parameters are unknown at the start, so they are estimated from the data. Most often the model describes the mean response expected for given predictor values, though sometimes the median or another quantile is used instead.

paragraphs.heading: Why it came first
paragraphs.text: Linear regression was the first kind of regression to be studied rigorously and put to wide practical use. One reason is that a model whose unknown parameters enter in a linear way is easier to fit. Another is that the statistical behaviour of the resulting estimates is easier to work out. Nonlinear regression is a generalization of it.

paragraphs.heading: Predicting new cases
paragraphs.text: A common goal is prediction or forecasting. You fit the model to an observed data set where both the predictors and the response were recorded. Later, if new predictor values arrive with no response attached, the fitted model can predict the response. In machine learning, linear regression counts as a supervised algorithm that learns from labelled data sets.

paragraphs.heading: How the model is fitted
paragraphs.text: The model is often fitted by least squares. There are other options, such as least absolute deviations, or ridge regression and lasso, which add a penalty to the least squares cost. Using the mean squared error as the cost gives large errors extra weight. In a data set with many large outliers, the model can then fit those outliers more than the true data, so a cost that is robust to outliers should be used there.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a coefficient
paragraphs.text: Each predictor x_j has a coefficient β_j. It is read as the expected change in y when x_j rises by one unit while every other predictor stays the same. People sometimes call this the unique effect of x_j on y. A predictor can have a large effect on its own yet nearly zero unique effect, which may mean another variable already captures its information. Care is needed, since some predictors cannot really be held fixed while others change.
